--- title: "Housing Prices Analysis 2020-Present" subtitle: "Cambridge Market Prices" author: "Pang Yoke Fei" date: "today" format: typst: toc: true number-sections: true papersize: a4 margin: x: 2cm y: 2cm fontsize: 10pt execute: echo: false warning: false --- # Why this report exists I bought a flat in Cambridge around 2022, and a few years on I want to know three things. Has it lost value? When, and at what price, should I sell it? And if I do sell, what would it take to move into a 2-3 bed freehold semi-detached or detached house in or around Cambridge? Rather than rely on gut feeling or estate agent chatter, I went to the public record. This report walks through the data, shows what I found, and ends with a plain-language summary of what I plan to do about it. # Importing the data & preparing parquet file The raw CSVs are large, so I converted them to a single parquet file once and read that from then on. ``` ::: ::: ## Schema of the dataset The data comes from the [UK Land Registry Price Paid Data](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/price-paid-data), which records every property sale in England and Wales. Each row is one sale, with details such as the price, the date, the postcode and the type of property. Here is what each column means: | Index | Column Name | Data Type | Description | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **0** | `transaction_id` | String | Unique identifier for the transaction (UUID wrapped in curly braces). | | **1** | `price` | Float | Transaction price in GBP (e.g., `450000`). | | **2** | `date_transferred` | String / Date | Date of transfer formatted as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM`. | | **3** | `postcode` | String | Property postcode (e.g., `CB1 2AB`). | | **4** | `property_type` | Categorical | `D` = Detached, `S` = Semi-Detached, `T` = Terraced, `F` = Flats/Maisonettes, `O` = Other. | | **5** | `new_build` | Categorical | `Y` = Newly built property, `N` = Established residential building. | | **6** | `tenure` | Categorical | `F` = Freehold, `L` = Leasehold. | | **7** | `paon` | String | Primary Addressable Object Name (typically house number or name). | | **8** | `saon` | String | Secondary Addressable Object Name (flat/apartment number). | | **9** | `street` | String | Street name. | | **10** | `locality` | String | Locality / Sub-district area. | | **11** | `town_city` | String | Town or City (e.g., `CAMBRIDGE`). | | **12** | `district` | String | Local authority district (e.g., `CAMBRIDGE` or `SOUTH CAMBRIDGESHIRE`). | | **13** | `county` | String | County (e.g., `CAMBRIDGESHIRE`). | | **14** | `ppd_category_type` | Categorical | `A` = Standard Price Paid entry, `B` = Additional Price Paid entry (non-standard transactions). | | **15** | `record_status` | Categorical | `A` = Addition, `C` = Change, `D` = Delete. | # Filtering the data and EDA ## Cities of Interest: `Cambridge`, `Royston`, `Saffron Walden`, and `Stevenage` I'm looking at four places: Cambridge itself, plus Royston, Saffron Walden and Stevenage, which are the commuter towns I'd realistically consider. Instead of throwing everything else away, I added a `city_interest` column that tags these four and labels the rest `OTHER`. That way I keep the wider market as context but can zoom in whenever I need to. ## Cleaning the Postcodes and Isolating the first part of the postcode Cambridge is not one uniform market, and a flat in CB1 behaves very differently from a house in CB22. To compare neighbourhoods later, I split each postcode and keep the first half (`CB1`, `CB2` and so on) in its own column. ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

A repossession or a sale to a company, for example, is not priced like an ordinary home sale. I only want ordinary sales, so I keep the standard ones (`ppd_category_type` of `A`) that are new records (`record_status` of `A`). A little context on the two categories: **Category A: Standard Sales** - Definition: Single residential properties sold for full market value. - Timeline: Collected by HM Land Registry from January 1, 1995 onwards. - Use Case: Represents the vast majority of normal, open-market home sales. **Category B: Additional Price Paid (APPD)** - Definition: Non-standard or specialized property transactions. - Timeline: Introduced and tracked starting October 14, 2013. - Included Transactions: - Repossessions and transfers under a power of sale - Buy-to-let properties flagged via a mortgage - Transfers to corporate or non-private owners - Properties classed under the "Other" category ### First, how many non-standard transactions are there? This chart shows the average sale price in each quarter since 2020, one line per city. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](eda-pdf_files/figure-typst/cell-7-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ### Quarterly average price faceted by feature An overall average hides a lot, because it blends cheap flats with expensive detached houses. So I split the same trend by property attribute. A small helper function keeps the three plots consistent. #### By property type `D` = Detached, `S` = Semi-Detached, `T` = Terraced, `F` = Flats/Maisonettes, `O` = Other. ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](eda-pdf_files/figure-typst/cell-9-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: #### By new build `Y` = Newly built, `N` = Established building. ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](eda-pdf_files/figure-typst/cell-10-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: #### By tenure `F` = Freehold, `L` = Leasehold. ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](eda-pdf_files/figure-typst/cell-11-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: ### Quarterly average price by postcode of interest Next I zoom in on specific neighbourhoods. These are the villages and towns around Cambridge that I would consider living in, along with their postcode districts. | Location | Postcode District | Post Town | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Trumpington** | CB2 | Cambridge | | **Great Shelford** | CB22 | Cambridge | | **Little Shelford** | CB22 | Cambridge | | **Sawston** | CB22 | Cambridge | | **Fulbourn** | CB21 | Cambridge | | **Girton** | CB3 | Cambridge | | **Great Chesterford** | CB10 | Saffron Walden | | **Saffron Walden** | CB10, CB11 | Saffron Walden | | **Royston** | SG8 | Royston | | **Newmarket** | CB8 | Newmarket | | **Bury St Edmunds** | IP32, IP33 | Bury St Edmunds | | **Bishop's Stortford** | CM22, CM23 | Bishop's Stortford | | **Hitchin** | SG4, SG5 | Hitchin | | **Letchworth Garden City** | SG6 | Letchworth Garden City | ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](eda-pdf_files/figure-typst/cell-12-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: Something jumped out at me here. Average prices for flats in CB2 (Trumpington) and CB22 (Great Shelford) have been falling since 2023, while other property types kept climbing. Girton tells a different story. It is a well-established village with a mix of property types, and flat prices in CB3 have held steady since 2023 while the other types rose. Flats there seem more resilient than in the newer areas. This matches what I see with my own eyes. Over the past few years Trumpington has seen a huge number of new houses and developments go up, and my hunch is that oversupply is pulling prices down. That is only a hunch, since the chart doesn't prove it, but it is enough to make me wary of buying in CB2 while the building continues. To test the hunch, I compared how many sales of each property type there were in Trumpington and in Girton. ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ::: {#inspect_sales_by_property_type .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

It is relatively affordable and has good transport links to both Cambridge and London. # Flat depreciation vs other property types **The question:** how have flat prices moved compared with other property types? The answer should help me decide when, and at what price, to sell the flat I bought around 2022 (four years ago), and what a 2-3 bed freehold semi-detached or detached house would cost in the cities I'm considering. A few ground rules for the numbers below: - I use **median** prices, which are not thrown off by a handful of very expensive sales. - Figures are in nominal GBP, so they are not adjusted for inflation. - 2026 is only a partial year (the data ends in August 2026), and recent sales are still being registered. Full-year comparisons therefore stop at 2025. ## Are flat prices falling? Sales volumes are also well below 2022 (about 920 a year, against about 540-575 in 2024-2025). In practice that means longer selling times and some haggling over price. # Finding a 2-3 bed freehold semi or detached house Now for the other half of the plan. ``` ::: ::: # Summary and recommendations Here is what I take away from all this. **Flats vs other types** 1. Flats have appreciated much less than houses since 2020. In Cambridge they have also lost value since 2023 (about -11%, or about -13% from the peak), while houses held their value or rose. 2. The Cambridge-wide median overstates the fall for resale flats (about +3% since 2022), because fewer expensive new builds are being sold now. The fair comparison is against resale figures for your own postcode district. 3. Prices have been stable since early 2024, so there is no evidence that waiting will bring a rebound. Volumes are low, so price realistically and be ready to negotiate. **Selling the flat** - The benchmark is resale flats in your postcode district (see the table above). Roughly flat since 2022 is the base case, though a new-build flat bought in 2022 may sell for less than was paid. - Cheaper commuter-belt flats (Stevenage at about £200-207k) are the only ones still creeping upward. - Monthly seasonality in the data is weak and noisy, so I wouldn't time the sale around it. **Buying a freehold 2-3 bed semi/detached** - Semis cost about £405-465k and have been flat for about two years, so there is no urgency. - The best value in resale semis is in **CB23/CB24/CB25 around Cambridge (about £375-380k), then SG2 Stevenage (about £385k) and SG8 Royston (about £405k)**. Saffron Walden is the most expensive of the four. - Buy resale, not new build, to avoid the roughly 14% premium. - A resale semi costs roughly £145k more than a resale flat in Cambridge, and £205-230k more in Royston, Stevenage and Saffron Walden (see the `upgrade` table). The flat's sale proceeds will need topping up, so run the `upgrade` table against your own budget. **Limitations** None of this is a valuation, and a few caveats are worth keeping in mind: - Medians describe typical sales, not any specific home. Size, condition, floor, lease length, service charge and street all matter, and none of them are in this dataset. - There is no bedroom count, so 2-3 bed is approximated by property type and price band. - Prices are nominal, so inflation makes the real picture weaker than shown. - 2026 data is partial and subject to registration lag, so recent quarters (especially 2026 new builds) may be revised.
